opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think of Timaeus as trying to bridge the gap between singular learning theory as a body of mathematics and something that's actually useful for making AI systems safer. SLT came out of Sumio Watanabe's work, and for a long time it was a fairly niche area of Bayesian statistics. It made claims about how learning works in models with degenerate geometry, which describes neural networks, but there wasn't much connecting it to the questions alignment people care about.

The bet behind Timaeus is that understanding the *structure* of a model, meaning what it's learned and how it generalizes, requires understanding how that structure develops during training. SLT gives you a principled handle on that. It tells you the geometry of the loss landscape, especially near degenerate critical points, is what governs which solutions a model ends up in and how it behaves out of distribution. If that's right, you want tools that measure that geometry in real models.

So a lot of our work has been building that toolkit. The local learning coefficient is the central example. It's a measure of effective model complexity, and we've found that tracking it over training lets you detect developmental stages, moments where the model reorganizes and acquires new structure. More recently we've been extending this to susceptibilities and related quantities, which ask how a model's internal structure responds to changes in the data distribution. That starts to look like a form of interpretability grounded in theory rather than in heuristics about individual neurons or features.

The way I'd put our role is a research program with three parts. First, test whether SLT's predictions hold up in practice on real networks, not just toy models. Second, turn the theory into scalable tools people can run on frontier-ish systems. Third, connect those tools to alignment problems: detecting when a model is learning something we didn't intend, understanding how training data shapes values and capabilities, and eventually having some ability to steer development rather than just inspect the end product.

I'd be the first to say there's a lot we don't know yet. Whether these methods scale cleanly, and how directly they plug into safety cases, are open questions. But I think alignment needs a science of how training data and training dynamics turn into model behavior, and SLT is one of the most promising foundations for that. Timaeus is trying to be the group that takes that seriously and does the empirical and engineering work needed to find out.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so Timaeus is the organization I co-founded, and the whole premise is basically a bet: that singular learning theory, and more broadly the kind of developmental, physics-flavored view of learning that SLT points toward, can be turned into tools that actually matter for alignment. Our job is to take that bet seriously and see how far it goes.

The way I think about it, there are sort of three layers to what we do. The first is the theory itself. SLT gives you a mathematically grounded story about how the geometry of the loss landscape, and specifically its singularities, controls what a neural network ends up learning. The key quantity there is the local learning coefficient, which you can think of as a measure of how complex the solution a model has found really is, in a way that's much more principled than counting parameters. A lot of our early work was just about making that quantity estimable in practice, for real networks, not just toy models.

The second layer is what we call developmental interpretability. The idea is that instead of only looking at a trained model and trying to reverse-engineer it, you watch how it forms over training. SLT predicts that learning should proceed through a series of phase transitions, where the model moves from one kind of solution to a qualitatively different one. If that's right, then those transitions are the natural places to look for the emergence of new structure, new capabilities, maybe new goals. We've found evidence of this in small transformers, where you can see the learning coefficient change at the same moments that the model's internal structure reorganizes. So we're trying to build the instrumentation to detect and characterize those moments.

And the third layer, which is really the point, is alignment. The hope is that if you understand the developmental trajectory, you get leverage. You can ask: when does deceptive or misaligned structure form, if it forms? Can you detect that early? Can you steer the training process away from it, or at least know when to intervene? That's a long way off, and I want to be honest that most of what we have today are tools and early results on small models rather than solutions. But I think the alignment field has been too short on fundamental science, and Timaeus exists to do that science, in a way that stays anchored to the actual problem rather than drifting into pure math for its own sake.

So the role, in a sentence, is to be the group that translates SLT from a beautiful theory about singular models into something a safety researcher can actually use. And to be ruthless about it: if the theory doesn't pay off empirically, we want to be the first to know.

astra-6.text:
I see TUS’s role as helping close the gap between singular learning theory as a mathematical framework and something that can actually help us understand neural networks. There’s a lot of work between having an interesting theory of learning and having a useful alignment tool.

The approach I’m excited about is to make that connection concrete: develop quantities we can estimate in real models, test what they tell us about the structure those models have learned, and see whether they help us understand changes during training. Then we can ask whether that understanding gives us better ways to detect or anticipate behavior we care about for alignment.

I wouldn’t say singular learning theory already gives us a solution to alignment. The role is more foundational: build the theory and the empirical methods together, and be clear about which connections to safety we’ve demonstrated and which are still hypotheses.

sol-6.1.text:
I see TUS’s role as helping bridge the gap between singular learning theory as a mathematical framework and something that can actually inform alignment work. The theory gives us a way to think about the structure of a model’s loss landscape and how that structure affects learning. But there’s still a lot of work involved in turning that into useful measurements and predictions for neural networks.

The direction I’m particularly excited about is developmental interpretability: understanding how a model acquires its internal structure over training. Can we identify transitions where a new capability or circuit emerges, and then understand what changed? Singular learning theory offers some tools for investigating that.

The alignment hope is that this eventually helps us understand and influence how models develop. But I’d distinguish that hope from what we’ve demonstrated. The immediate job is to make the connection between the mathematics and the experiments solid enough that we can tell where the theory is useful.
